title: Force and Motion
description: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can make objects start moving, stop, or change direction. Mass and force both affect how objects move.

exercises.question: What is a FORCE?
exercises.exp: A force is a push or a pull that can make things move or stop moving.

exercises.question: Kicking a soccer ball is an example of a ___.
exercises.exp: A kick is a push — your foot pushes the ball forward.

exercises.question: Opening a door uses a ___.
choices: push or pull depending on the door
exercises.exp: Some doors you push open and some you pull open — both use force!

exercises.question: Which object would be HARDEST to push across the floor?
exercises.exp: More mass means you need more force. A heavy box needs a lot of force to push.

exercises.question: A toy car rolls across the floor and stops. What slowed it down?
exercises.exp: Friction is a force between the wheels and floor that slows the car down.

exercises.question: Which object is moving the FASTEST?
exercises.exp: A cheetah can run up to 120 km/h — the fastest land animal!

exercises.question: Gravity is a force that ___.
exercises.exp: Gravity pulls everything toward the centre of Earth — that is why things fall down!

exercises.question: A bigger PUSH makes a ball travel ___.
exercises.exp: More force = more speed and distance. A hard throw goes farther than a gentle one.

exercises.question: Which shows a PULL?
exercises.exp: Picking up a backpack pulls it upward toward you — that is a pull!

exercises.question: Two toy cars race. Car A takes 5 seconds and Car B takes 3 seconds. Which is faster?
exercises.exp: Less time = more speed. Car B finished faster, so it is the faster car!

exercises.question: What does FRICTION do?
exercises.exp: Friction is a force that opposes motion — it slows things down and creates heat.

exercises.question: A ball rolls in a STRAIGHT LINE, then hits a wall and changes direction. What changed it?
exercises.exp: The wall pushed back on the ball (a force!) making it change direction.

exercises.question: A sled slides down a snowy hill. Which force pulls it downhill?
exercises.exp: Gravity pulls the sled (and everything!) toward Earth's centre — that is why sleds go DOWN hills, not up!

exercises.question: Which surface would a ball roll FARTHEST on before stopping?
exercises.exp: Less friction = longer roll. Smooth tile has much less friction than carpet or gravel!

exercises.question: What happens to a moving object if there is NO friction at all?
choices: it keeps moving forever at the same speed
exercises.exp: Without friction, nothing stops a moving object! In space, objects keep moving forever — no friction to slow them down.

exercises.question: Pulling a suitcase with a handle uses a ___.
exercises.exp: Dragging a suitcase by its handle pulls it toward you — a pull force!

exercises.question: You push a book across a table. It slows and stops. Which force stopped it?
choices: air resistance and friction from the table
the book's own weight pushing down only
exercises.exp: Friction between the book and table surface slows the book. Air resistance also acts against moving objects!

exercises.question: Which of these moves in a CURVED path?
choices: a book sliding off a table in a straight line
a ball thrown in the air (gravity curves its path)
a car moving along a straight road
exercises.exp: A thrown ball curves downward due to gravity — it moves in a curved path called a parabola!

exercises.question: Two students push a box from OPPOSITE sides with equal force. The box ___.
exercises.exp: Equal forces from opposite sides cancel out — balanced forces mean no change in motion. The box stays still!

exercises.question: A heavy truck and a small car drive at the SAME speed and brake at the same time. Which stops faster?
choices: they stop at exactly the same time
the small car stops faster — less mass needs less force
exercises.exp: The lighter car has less mass and less momentum — it needs less force to stop so it stops more quickly.

exercises.question: What is SPEED?
choices: the distance an object travels in a certain amount of time
the colour of a moving object
the direction an object is facing
exercises.exp: Speed = distance ÷ time. A car travelling 60 km in 1 hour has a speed of 60 km/h!

exercises.question: A feather and a rock are dropped from the same height. On Earth, the rock hits the ground first. Why?
choices: air resistance slows the feather much more than the heavier rock
the feather is afraid of falling
exercises.exp: Air resistance (a friction-like force from air) affects the feather much more than the heavy rock — the rock falls faster!

exercises.question: When you squeeze the BRAKES on a bicycle, what forces are acting?
choices: friction between brake pads and wheels slows the bicycle
exercises.exp: Brake pads press on the wheel rim creating friction — this friction force slows and stops the bicycle.

exercises.question: Which correctly matches the TYPE of force with an example?
choices: push: kicking a ball away from you
exercises.exp: Kicking a ball pushes it away from your foot — that is a push force! The foot pushes the ball forward.

exercises.question: A spacecraft in deep space has no gravity and no air. What keeps it moving?
choices: inertia — objects in motion stay in motion without a force to stop them
exercises.exp: In space with no friction or gravity, a spacecraft keeps moving at the same speed forever — this is inertia at work!

exercises.question: You push two boxes. Box A weighs 2 kg, Box B weighs 10 kg. Which needs MORE force to move?
choices: Box B — more mass needs more force to accelerate
exercises.exp: More mass = more force needed to move it. Box B (10 kg) needs 5× more force than Box A (2 kg).

exercises.question: Which of the following is NOT a contact force?
choices: the push of your hand on a door
the pull of a rope in tug-of-war
exercises.exp: Gravity acts at a distance — it pulls objects toward Earth without touching them. Friction, pushes, and pulls require contact.

exercises.question: A ball is rolling and you PUSH it in the SAME direction it is moving. What happens?
exercises.exp: A push in the same direction as motion adds to the ball's speed — it goes faster!

exercises.question: Skydivers jump from a plane and fall. They open a PARACHUTE. What happens next?
choices: they slow down — the parachute increases air resistance
exercises.exp: A large parachute catches lots of air — this increases air resistance (a force opposing motion) and slows the fall.

exercises.question: Which of the following is an example of GRAVITY helping us?
choices: making it hard to carry heavy bags
keeping us on the ground and making rivers flow downhill
exercises.exp: Gravity keeps us on Earth, makes rivers flow downhill, and keeps planets orbiting — incredibly useful force!

exercises.question: A toy train goes around a circular track. What force keeps it on the curved track?
choices: the push of the track's curved wall against the train (normal force)
exercises.exp: The curved track wall pushes inward on the train — this centripetal force keeps it on the circular path!

exercises.question: A push or a pull is called a ___.
exercises.exp: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can change an object's speed, direction, or shape!

exercises.question: What unit is used to measure force?
exercises.exp: Force is measured in newtons (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton who studied forces and gravity!

exercises.question: If TWO equal forces push an object in OPPOSITE directions, the object ___.
choices: stays still — the forces are balanced
exercises.exp: Equal and opposite forces cancel each other out — this is a balanced force and the object does not move (or stays at constant speed).

exercises.question: An UNBALANCED force will ___.
choices: cause an object to change its speed or direction
exercises.exp: Unbalanced forces cause a change in motion — the object will accelerate, decelerate, or change direction!

exercises.question: What force pulls objects toward the centre of the Earth?
exercises.exp: Gravity is the force that pulls all objects toward Earth's centre — it is what gives objects weight!

exercises.question: Friction is a force that ___.
choices: acts against motion, slowing things down
exercises.exp: Friction is a force that opposes motion — it acts in the opposite direction to movement. Rough surfaces have more friction.

exercises.question: Which surface creates MORE friction?
exercises.exp: Rough sandpaper creates lots of friction — the rough surfaces grip together. Smooth or slippery surfaces have much less friction.

exercises.question: You are pushing a heavy box across the floor. Which would make pushing EASIER?
choices: adding more weight to the box
exercises.exp: Wheels reduce friction — they roll instead of slide. That is why people invented wheels to move heavy things easily!

exercises.question: What do we call the force of gravity on an object?
exercises.exp: Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object. On Earth, a 1 kg object weighs about 9.8 newtons.

exercises.question: On the MOON, gravity is weaker than on Earth. You would ___.
choices: weigh the same as on Earth
have no mass on the moon
exercises.exp: The moon has weaker gravity (about 1/6 of Earth's). You would weigh 6 times less — perfect for high jumps!

exercises.question: A feather and a hammer are dropped from the same height on the MOON (no air). Which lands first?
choices: they land at exactly the same time
exercises.exp: With no air resistance, gravity pulls all objects equally regardless of mass — both land at exactly the same time! (Proven by Apollo astronauts!)

exercises.question: What happens to friction between a bicycle tyre and the road when the road is WET?
choices: friction decreases — wet roads are slippery
exercises.exp: Water acts as a lubricant between tyre and road — reducing friction. That is why wet roads are more slippery and dangerous!

exercises.question: A car is moving at constant speed on a straight road. The forces on it are ___.
choices: balanced — engine force equals friction and air resistance
exercises.exp: Constant speed means balanced forces — the engine's forward push exactly equals friction and air resistance pushing backward.

exercises.question: Air resistance is a type of ___.
choices: friction force between air and a moving object
exercises.exp: Air resistance is friction between a moving object and the air. It acts opposite to the direction of movement.

exercises.question: Which shape reduces air resistance on a fast car?
exercises.exp: Streamlined shapes let air flow smoothly around them — reducing drag (air resistance). Racing cars and planes use streamlined designs!

exercises.question: A ball is thrown upward. As it rises, gravity ___.
exercises.exp: Gravity always pulls downward. As the ball rises against gravity, it slows down. At the top, it stops and falls back down.

exercises.question: What is SPEED?
choices: the distance an object travels per unit of time
the force acting on an object
exercises.exp: Speed = distance ÷ time. For example, 100 metres in 10 seconds = 10 m/s speed.

exercises.question: Which of these has the MOST air resistance?
exercises.exp: A parachute is designed to have maximum air resistance — this is what slows the fall and makes landing safe!

exercises.question: Newton's First Law says an object at rest stays at rest UNLESS ___.
choices: an unbalanced force acts on it
exercises.exp: Newton's 1st Law: objects stay still (or keep moving at the same speed) until an unbalanced force changes their state!

exercises.question: A football is kicked and rolls across grass. It eventually stops. Why?
choices: the ball runs out of force
friction from the grass and air resistance slow it down
it gets heavier as it rolls
exercises.exp: Friction between the ball and grass, plus air resistance, gradually removes energy from the ball — eventually it stops.
